utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall continue this morning with the evidence of Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Lukic will continue in a moment. I have to remind you that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll try to proceed more quickly than yesterday because our time is limited. You started telling us yesterday, but please be brief, what was your position, was it in the interest of the police and the Army of Yugoslavia for the Albanian civilians to move out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a single indication from any quarters nor was it the intent of not only the state authorities but any other agency of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. All citizens were equal in our eyes, and I would say that Albanians were even more privileged than any other community.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With the leaders, the elders of the Albanian community, did you try to negotiate with agree and what did you achieve in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the well-known events in Likosane the liquidation of Adem Jashari when the problems in that municipality got very complicated, when there were daily demonstrations and meetings of all kinds of associations and citizens unions, the elders of the village came to me offering a handshake of friendship and the transparency of the Republic of Serbia came to the fore and we managed to come to a gentleman's agreement, namely, that all the elders of the community in the Pristina area - and I have to say again that in the Glogovac municipality that my police station covered there was not a single Serb, everybody was Albanian. So for the sake of peace in the household, they undertook - and I'm talking about the beginning of 1998 - they promised that they would not give logistical support to Siptar terrorist gangs, extremists, and so on, that we would be able to move around peacefully, at least move through the centre of the village towards our base, and wherever they had any problem we would come to their aid and we would try to accommodate them in every situation. That was our mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give us the names of specific villages whose elders came to you to talk.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from Komorane village which is a junction on the Pristina-Pec road, starting from Komorane we talked to Idriz Nishori, a very loyal citizen, and the terrorists even tried to assassinate him. He got out with multiple wounds, and then as you move on towards Glogovac and make a turn from Donje Zabelj, and Koretica, we talked to Xhemajl Rexhepi which is his real name, he owned a petrol station in Poklek, he himself is from Koretica. Then there was Tuf Dina [phoen] in Koretica we named him all communist, which was sort of a term of endearment. With all of these people we came to a gentlemen's agreement and they all together came to see me and there was the deputy director of Jukos in Drenica, in Globare. You can find that on the map, his name is Skender, I forget his last name, he was deputy director of that plant. They all came together to see me and they asked for my word of honour that I would meet them at the right time because you know how it is if anybody was noticed coming into a police station or coming out that person would be liquidated and their family would be targeted. So I had to organize these meetings in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now in 1999, again in relation to the movements of population, are you aware of the influence, if any, of the KLA on the movement of civilian population; if you have such knowledge, tell us how.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, but even back in mid-1998, the KLA was very influential in the area of the Glogovac municipality, not in the sense that they enjoyed respect for their qualities, but they had spread fear among the population by terrorist means and people had to obey them. In 1998, so that you can understand the chronology, when the roads were being deblocked, even then on the orders of Siptar terrorists individual groups and tribes were very obedient to the KLA and followed the orders of the terrorists, and all this was repeated in 1999. But this time it was not individual groups and tribes but all of the people concerned by the air-strikes started looking for shelters, for safe areas. The terrorists asked them to create the appearance of a humanitarian catastrophe, and the NATO air-strikes were a reality. So they were really in an unenviable position. They moved from village to village, they moved out to the woods into hilly areas where they thought they were safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try, did you make any personal efforts, to prevent the civilians from leaving Glogovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the purposes of our existence in Glogovac municipality, and the orders from upstairs were to try to convince people to stay at home to tell them they would enjoy every protection we are able to offer, that we would share a common fate because together we are stronger, as they say. And all the citizens who had any respect for us as human beings and professionals went along with that, even those people who belonged to families, some members of which were in the KLA but however, most of them had to obey KLA orders and to create this humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of some villages where you offered your protection and tried to persuade people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With my colleagues, commanding officers, the CO of the operative personnel, we visited every village we had access to from Trstenik and Globare towards Strbulovo, Domenik and the road from Glogovac, Komorane. There are several villages there, Donje Poklek, Gornje Poklek, Donje Zabelj, Koretica, Komorane. On many occasions we would run into people, women, children, the elderly, moving ahead like headless chicken, and I knew those people well. Hamza Hajra was one of the elders, one of the renowned people of that community I met; then there was the former policeman, late policeman, his name eludes me at the moment. We talked directly to those who didn't know a word of Serbian and he gave them his word of honour that they would be safe. We did have some success and I can tell you for a fact that there was not a single case of migration in the residential areas in Glogovac. In all the time I was in the Glogovac municipality, I don't know of a single case that somebody moved out from that area, except for extremist villages, Trpeza, Kisna Reka, and the area in lower Drenica, that is, from Poluze towards Banjica. Those were extremist villages in the hilly areas where we had much less influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the incident in Trstenik when the people started leaving, when was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On two occasions, once it was during a joint action of the army and the police, I believe it was in September 1998; and then on two occasions the same thing happened in 1999 in the area between Trstenik village and over there towards Strbulovo we ran into larger groups, hundreds, I would say, of people who didn't even know where they were going. They would spend some time in one village and then the local residents would tell them, We've had enough, we don't have enough food to share with you to keep you here any longer, plus you are increasing the danger for us. And we managed, even my humble self, I don't want to indulge in any false modesty, we managed to persuade those people to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any reports saying that the police were driving civilians out of Glogovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again with full responsibility, I guarantee with my life and with my honour that nothing like that happened during my tenure and we value our word highly, at least those of us with patriarchal upbringing in that area. God as my witness, even young people came to my station, to my office, I offered them coffee and juice. We talked in a very friendly way, they were very concerned, very afraid. I watched my police officers carefully, trying to discern any signs of violation of the usual rules of treatment of the Albanian community, and I can say with full responsibility that our police officers acted with dignity and fairness, like true ambassadors of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that any police units turned back large groups of civilians trying to leave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, there were many actions to suppress terrorism in the broader area of Glogovac, so the PJP sometimes ran into large groups of civilian population on trucks, on trailers, whatever they had they would bring those citizens. Then I would assign a police patrol to escort them back to the place where they lived normally or to another place where they had family and they felt safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now those units on the ground, apart from the fact that they turned back civilians and told them to go home, did they also bring large groups of people for you to question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PJP, according to their work-plan and programme, in those places that held strongholds of terrorists that's where they were the most active, that's the area of Cicavica, Mount Cicavica on one side, and on the other side Likovac, Gornje Obrinje, Donje Obrinje, Ovcarevo, up to Banjica, Negrovac, and so on. In that initial period already in 1998, those two months when we were deblocking roads, once or twice they brought larger groups like dozens of people who were found in the area of those so-called combat actions. We used our police methods to establish whether any of those people brought in had really participated in any terrorist attacks or not. For that purpose our colleagues from SUP Pristina who are specially trained for that, expert teams from the crime police and scenes of crime officers, because as I said yesterday our personnel was limited in that way, we did not have such expert teams ourselves. They checked, verified, questioned, used forensic methods such as the paraffin glove test to establish which among those people might have shot previously at police officers. And in each such group of between 10 and 20 people, there were some who were identified as participants in terrorist attacks, that is, members of the KLA, and they would be taken into custody and transferred to SUP Pristina. I don't know whether it was to the public security or the state security sector there, I don't know that part. And they were prosecuted and I don't know what later happened to them, but I believe they were all amnestied when that amnesty was in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where did you hold those large groups of citizens and where did you question them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether in my examination yesterday I explained in greater detail about our premises and the conditions in which we worked in Glogovac because our police station was a make-shift building, it was a pre-fab building. The largest office in there was my office, it was upstairs. The other offices were really very small, 3 by 3 or 3 by 2, and there was a classroom on the ground floor, it was about 5 by 4 metres. So it was a pre-fab building and the conditions did not exist there to hold larger groups of people. In those exceptional circumstances that we faced when large groups of people would be brought in, maybe up to 200 people following the police and military actions, so groups would be between 200 and in some cases, as far as I can recall, there were up to 500 people, people who would be brought in in a single day applying the methods that I just described. And since the municipality building is right next door to the police building and there is the culture hall right next door, it is a big hall, it used to be -- it used to be used as a cinema, and it was a large room that could accommodate about 600 people in the audience, there were chairs there, there was the scene. So the conditions there were excellent. On those occasions when larger groups of people would be brought in, we would put them there temporarily and the interviews would be held in the official premises of the OUP Glogovac, we would do it group by group because it was the only place where it was possible to conduct such interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, were there any cases when the military would bring in these terrorist suspects?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you treated them in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the treatment was the same, regardless of whether it was the police or the army, they would bring in those larger groups by truck, they would hand them over to us, and this was the system that I put in place. I think that there is -- there are records of it somewhere, unless of course some of them have been destroyed because of the war. I always demanded that a list, an exhaustive list of all the people who were brought in be made with all their personal details. I wanted the exact time when they were handed over stated there and the exact time when they were released, because at that time, before the state of war was declared, we applied the Law on Criminal Procedure and we had a right to detain them for three days. And in that time, regardless of the number of persons in custody, we had to do our job, we had to finish our job. And with the assistance of the -- our colleagues from the state security sector and the Pristina SUP there were limited numbers of the former, but we managed to complete this job within two or three days to do the paraffin glove or gun-shot residue tests and to release all of those people to their homes, with the exception of those who had been proven to be members of the KLA, and then they were handed over to Pristina, to the SUP Pristina. I don't know whether they were handed over to the public security sector or the state security sector, this is not something of my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try to do some yes-and-no answers now. Were there any volunteers in your OUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any paramilitary or parapolice forces in your area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What security forces were deployed in your OUP area?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exclusively members of the police and of the Yugoslav Army, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many VJ troops were deployed in the area of your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really count them and that was not my duty, but they were moving around that area. First of all, as they say, based on my experience because I held that ground there, after the NATO aggression, after the air-strikes began, the angel of mercy, as they called it, that day or the next day the first troops that arrived arrived from the direction of Srbica, and I think those were the units from Raska, and I couldn't really give you the designation of those units because I might be wrong and I don't want to make mistakes. So they held the Srbica-Glogovac road. At the beginning the staff command for the Glogovac municipality was located in the village of Trstenik, and I talked, as far as I can recall, on several occasions with Lieutenant-Colonel, I believe, Dikovic, who was there with a group of his associates, so I talked to him several times. And later on the headquarters was moved to Globare, closer to the centre of Glogovac. And those units all gravitated to the town, the units went there and their headquarters was in Globare and in Trstenik. And on the other side, in the direction of the border, those units that were from Raska or whatever you want to call it, and from the level crossing in the direction of Poklek and Zabelj, this area was covered by personnel from the Pristina Corps. And they were deployed -- they were billeted in houses, various buildings in that area. So the military forces from the Raska area were up to Globare, up to one side of Glogovac; and on the other side, just to make things clearer, from Poklek towards Komorane, the Pristina-Pec road, that area was held by the Pristina Corps troops. I was able to observe that every day, that's why I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any anti-terrorist actions carried out in your area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I testified yesterday and here today, this was the very epicentre of terrorism in the whole of Kosovo and Metohija, in particular the area around the Cicavica and below Cicavica, the village of Gradica -- well, it is a well-known fact that there were all those tribes and the families of Mehmet Gradica and Jusufi who used to be a well-known collaborationist with Germany and there was also a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would please answer the question, were any anti-terrorist actions carried out in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I was about to say, the most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do not respond in that way to me. You were clearly not answering the question. Please now answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in a word, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The police officers from your OUP, did they participate in those actions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you know whether any PJP members participated in anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You as the chief of the OUP, were you able to order anything to the PJP personnel when they were in combat mission?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did PJP members report to you about the course of the action?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to those actions, did you receive any reports or any information about anything?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any attempts on the part of the VJ personnel to subordinate all OUP Glogovac personnel to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who came to see you and what did this look like?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a yes or no answer to that, so if I'm allowed to give you a broader description. I was issued an order by a military patrol sometime in spring to go to the command post in Trstenik and to report to Lieutenant-Colonel, well, Dikovic, yes, my brain blocked for a while, for a meeting that would be held in the morning at about 8.00 about the resubordination to the army command in accordance with the rules that were in force. In the morning I and my colleague, inspector Milutin Tomcic, went there, we complied with the summons. I expressed my gratitude and I greeted Lieutenant-Colonel Dikovic and his colleagues from the military; but at the same time I explained to them that this was an OUP that's dealing with administrative issues and that we have a limited number of police officers, and that I cannot independently make any such decisions about any subordination, that this had to be done at a higher level. They heard what I had to say, they understood my views, they thanked me, and I went back the same day. I didn't even sit down, I went back to the Glogovac OUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So did you subordinate yourself to the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the army officers talk to you and give you any requests regarding the clear-up operations of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a man by the name of Rade Krsmanovic, as far as I can remember, came down to see me, I was in contact with him. He was a captain, and there was another colleague of his, they came to see me about the clear-up operations. I really respect them but I can't recall all of their names. I think that this other man was a Muslim. I don't know his name. They were very correct in their behaviour. I listened to them and I explained to them what the situation was like. I told them that in the area of operations of the army, that this was something that was within the jurisdiction of the officer in charge of the operation and not of the local police station, which is what we were. On the other hand, I explained to them - and I hope that they understood - that the local government, the Glogovac municipality, had stopped functioning at the time when terrorist actions escalated, and it closed down at the time when NATO air-strikes began and all the way up to mid-April when at the request of their superior some of the people from the municipality came back. So we did not have the utilities, we didn't have the Crisis Staff in our municipality, we didn't have civilian protection, we didn't have any assets to put at their disposal. And the OUP Glogovac did not have a single truck at its disposal. So we were limited in terms of our equipment, we couldn't provide any assistance of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5D1031 up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you have it in your binder, 5D1031. Yes, we have it on our screens now. Tell me now, in the Glogovac OUP area, who patrolled the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me just read this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This pertains to check-points, and now I'm asking you whether you know about patrols.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I do apologise. As far as patrols are concerned, we from the Glogovac OUP patrolled the road that we could use at that time and that was the road from Globare towards Komorane, to the left and to the right, the Pec-Pristina main road, and all the way to the border of the Glogovac municipality. So from Kijevo or Gornje Koretica, towards Kosovo Polje and up the road to Djurdjica which is closer to Kijevo, that's the border with the Klina municipality and the main, or rather, the local road from Komorane to Fustica in the direction of the municipality of Lipljan, and in the depth towards Srbica, this was more an area where the VJ was in charge because this is where their Main Staff was and this was the area that they patrolled. And we couldn't move into the depth and they could, they had the appropriate assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1999 on the road from Pristina to Glogovac were there any check-points; and if so, whose check-points?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some, for instance, in Slatina itself, there was a check-point at the intersection forking off towards the airport held by the army; then on the roads towards farms from Krivovo towards Komorane there were chicken farms there and there was another check-point, also military in Komorane. Up until the air-strikes there was a police check-point, that was one that was -- had been in existence for years held by the police. And there was another one in the area jointly military and police check-point. After the roads were deblocked and that clash with the terrorists in Lapusnik after that place was liberated from the large number of terrorists who had held it, there was another check-point of the police held, manned, by the PJP. That's what I know. Now, further inland towards Domenik and from Globare towards Srbica, that was the responsibility of the army because only the army was equipped to hold that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your reference to PJP check-point after the liberation of Lapusnik a reference to 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From September, from end September, when Lapusnik was already liberated, from that time onwards. Let's say from October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "October," which year?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 1998, that was the time when our forces already controlled Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. I now would like to know about the uniforms worn by the police who worked in OUP Glogovac in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All police officers, and I as the chief, had to wear exclusively blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What villages in your territory held the best fortified strongholds of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll describe it by naming roads or routes. That borderline from Glogovac -- between Glogovac and Srbica, from that point towards Likosane and then again deeper inland towards Grabovac, and on the right side looking from Glogovac towards Obrinje, Trdevac, Likovac, and then from that point towards Glogovac another terrorist stronghold was in Trstenik, Sakici brothers, five of them, were a separate terrorist group that shot at the police frequently, including myself; however, I survived and I'm still here to tell you about it today. In Banjica there were larger terrorist units because it's a wooded, hilly area providing good hiding places. There was Mount Kosmaca was where Selman Selmani, nicknamed Sultan, held a sway and held everyone in fear. He was practically the ruler of that area, and then there was Jakup Krasniqi, at that time he was the spokesperson and now he's the Speaker of the Parliament of Kosovo, he had organized the entire village population to do the digging, guards duty, and in that village Shaban Shala was another self-styled commander I believe, old, experienced illegal politician who was in charge of Obrovac, whereas Jakup Krasniqi moved to Malisevo to the KLA headquarters, where he was in the Main Staff with the current prime minister of Kosovo, Hashim Thaqi, and he commanded that area. Now, across the road from there towards the Pristina-Pec road from Komorane towards Kisna Reka and Trpeza all the villages there were terrorist villages and their centres were Novo Selo and Berisa. They tied in with that Crnoljevo mountains across Fustica and Sedlare, that's the locality of Klecka, those are all the strongholds I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you. If a policeman were responsible for a disciplinary infraction, would he be subject to disciplinary proceedings and who would conduct these proceedings before the air-strikes and after the beginning of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to maintain good discipline among the police, we had to raise the level of liability. Every infraction, every violation, was subject to punishment. For minor infractions it was the chief of secretariat who would decide what measures to take, it was Borko Pekic [phoen] at the time, being late for work, unkempt in appearance, et cetera. More serious violations such as theft, violation of combat-readiness or anything else, especially where arson and theft were concerned, disciplinary proceedings would be held within the framework of the secretariat where we have a disciplinary court, that is the first-instance court. And then in the second instance there was the disciplinary court at the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. You can find more details from documentation. I cannot tell you more about it offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you about Abdullah Salihu, who had testified here before. Was there a person in Glogovac, a police officer named Momo Peljevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Begovic"]?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been working since 1994 [as interpreted], and I have worked in OUP Lipljan and SUP Pristina and Glogovac, and I held for a while the area of Podujevo. I can say with full responsibility that there was no police inspector of that name, and such -- we don't have anyone by that name. It must be somebody's fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript was it 1994 that you started working or earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about the broader question, does the name Momo Begovic mean anything at all to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's also wrong then I see, it's not Begovic, it's Peljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean -- that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I wasn't quite clear in my answer. That name means nothing to me because there was no such person in SUP Pristina ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know Abdullah Salihu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time I hear that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time did you hear about the killing in Glogovac of Rahman Topilla?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name doesn't ring a bell either, and of course if I haven't heard of the man I haven't heard of the killing either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You tried several times yesterday to tell us and I interrupted you every time, promising that we would come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 6D112, and we need page 2 in English and page 3 in Serbian. I'm sorry, we need first pages to begin with to see what this document is all about. Can we get in Serbian the first page too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see what document this is, although some letters are missing in Serbian, but it's a document of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, dated 12th March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's an OSCE report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we have page 2 in English and page 3 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you read the first line.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 4th of March, the KLA informed OSCE verifiers that they would not accept a police presence in the territory that they control between Srbica and Glogovac and that they would attack any police convoy attempting to pass through the area. KLA reinforcements were observed in that area. The tension was reduced when the police announced that they had postponed an intended convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I remember, and I explained I think yesterday that the OSCE representative warned me personally, among others, that I should by no means send my forces there because a conflict was inevitable if I did and he had been given that message by Sami Lushtaku, the commander for the broader area of Drenica. And indeed, following the cue of the OSCE, we did not send our forces to that area along that route, we avoided it even before; but now after this word from the OSCE and this confirmation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one -- yesterday you told us that that was on the 17th of November, 1998. Is that correct? I'm not misunderstanding your evidence from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just tied it in with this issue that even before the OSCE had made such suggestions, but this item confirms why we were not able to and why we didn't dare, to be frank, to patrol there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask you a different question. When was it the KVM representative spoke to you and told you to stay away from the road between Glogovac and Srbica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just after they arrived in Glogovac from October. In November there were more frequent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've understood you correctly. That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you read paragraph 3 then, beginning with the words: "On 5th March ..."

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On 5th March there was an explosion" -- sorry. "On the 5th of March, approximately 15 to 20 KLA members ambushed a police patrol in an area south-west of Pristina airport. According to police sources, 11 policemen were wounded, six of them seriously, and two police vehicles were destroyed by rocket-propelled grenades."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in the area of your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Vasiljevo group that belonged to the brigade of Fehmi Lladrovci, actually it belonged to one of the battalions, one of them -- several battalions within that brigade, 114th Brigade of Fehmi Lladrovci, that's the group that mounted this attack that caused fatalities, as we can see. It's not an isolated case. This happened in March. They escalated later all the way up to the Rambouillet negotiations, but I'm not going into politics now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After mid-April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just -- before you move off this if you're moving onto a different subject, there's another event referred to there which you presumably have knowledge of -- in fact, there are two. There's one on the 7th of March where policemen were killed and a third was wounded. You see that? Are you familiar with that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is referred to is a suburb of Pristina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's outwith your area, yeah. Sorry. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. When we are on this subject, we have 21 terrorist attacks in the area of Glogovac, but since the police officers killed in those actions are not from Glogovac OUP, we didn't ask this witness about these actions. So I would kindly ask your guidance how to proceed in this matter. Should I just list the evidence we have on these issues or just in writing submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these all attacks reflected in the -- in this report as --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- occurring between the talks?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's attacks since August until May, since August 1998 until the end of May 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are all reflected in documents, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are these documents already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what context were they exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's our famous 6D614 document, and we have other documents as well, but when -- the gentleman's told us yesterday that he didn't register police officers killed in his area unless they are from his OUP. So he was aware of killings of other police officers, but they admitted that they didn't register those police officers coming from other SUPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying he has personal knowledge of these various events however?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It would take too much time I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but does he have personal knowledge of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that he knows about one for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is exactly the sort of situation which should be dealt with in a 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because it saves all the time and it allows him to confirm his personal knowledge and it enhances the value of the documentary record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have it the next week, but with this witness we missed the chance to go that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there is one that the witness knows about for sure, you may be well-advised to at least put that one to him. I'll think further about the others and if there is any guidance that we think can usefully be given to you we'll give it to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have 6D614 put up in e-court, page 704. We need item 601 -- I apologise, 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, do you recall the killing of these six policemen?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 704, item 600.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember this incident exceptionally well, even until present. I remember it so graphically since I never saw anything like it, not even in the horror movies I saw. It says here the 1st of April, 1999, in the village of Trstenik, which is along the road between Globare and Trstenik, closer to Trstenik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether these were members of your OUP.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the secretariat in Kragujevac. They were in a freight vehicle, it was an official vehicle, and they were patrolling the stretch between Globare and Trstenik. Since it is a bad road, it's a regional motorway, and just prior to that there was heavy rain, in one of the puddles in the middle of the road the terrorists planted an anti-tank mine. It was a Niva vehicle. It went over the anti-tank mine, and we found pieces of their bodies 1 to 200 metres away, a fist, parts of the skull, and so on. There was so many deaths in just a single day, this was not the only case. By sheer circumstance I was also witness to this particular incident. I can go into details if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English version it's completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have we got the right page?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, he said page 704, is that in B/C/S. What is the English page, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 704, all pages in this document are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 704, all pages are the same in this document. I was just informed that this page might not be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there only is the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying you were an eye-witness to this, Mr. Damjanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. We were collecting the body parts in the fields nearby, hands, fists, legs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After the event. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, in the territory of your secretariat after the 15th of April, 1999, did you have occasion to see the police and military sporting any ribbons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a binding instruction in place since terrorists were introduced in the area. Several of our colleagues' uniforms were seized by them, and under such circumstances they could pretend to be someone else. That's why we were obliged to wear ribbons on our left shoulder. I think we used three colours, red, blue, and yellow, and then daily we would be informed which colour, and we used those for the purpose of identifying our members. As far as I recall in that period as of mid-April, the military usually wore only a single ribbon and not three like we did. If I remember correctly, they were wearing red ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While in Glogovac did you ever see or hear that the police at check-points manned together with the Army of Yugoslavia tolerate the behaviour of other policemen, killing, looting, and doing similar things?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess it's a fair question on your part, but it is -- it has nothing with common sense. There were no such events. I never heard of it and I wouldn't be able to comprehend it. Imagine two institutions, two bodies, at the same check-point and one of the sides not reacting to such behaviour of the other. That would be highly inappropriate. I have never heard of such cases and I don't believe that would have been possible, to put it briefly. And I never received such information either orally or in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Damjanac. I have no questions for you at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Damjanac. A few questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 6D579 in e-court, page 2, please -- excuse me, this page. Could we please zoom in in the B/C/S version so that the witness can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, a few moments ago you said that the army wore red ribbons as far as you can recall during 1999. This is an instruction to the police for wearing identification bands in May. Please have a look. I believe it says on certain days police members were supposed to wear red bands as well.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you seem to misunderstand me. I was very precise. We had three colours. I used to wear them on a daily basis, red, yellow, blue, and we changed them. On one day we would have red, on the next day yellow, and on the third day blue. I don't know how you interpret this, but I think it's simply enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I understood you, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom out in the B/C/S version and could we please see the bottom of the page. I'm interested in the remark at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please read it out.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Remark: The Yugoslav Army does not have identification ribbons."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, in English on the document, that has been translated differently, it's translated as "identification bands." Is there any significance in that at all or is the word in Serbian a word that could mean either ribbon or band?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in Serbian literally it would be band. The title says: "Instruction to the police for wearing identification bands in May." And in the remark it says VJ did not have identification bands. In Serbian it is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But yet when the witness read it, it was translated as "identification ribbons." All right. Thank you very much. If -- Mr. Damjanac, if Mr. Lukic wants to explore the matter further with you then that will be open to him when he has an opportunity to ask you further questions at the end of your evidence. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Damjanac, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic and I represent General Lazarevic as his Defence counsel, and I have just a few questions for you. Yesterday and today you told us about many cases of those brutal terrorist attacks on citizens and military and police personnel. What I'm interested in is whether those attacks escalated significantly once the OSCE mission pulled out of Kosovo and Metohija. Just very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mission pulled out I think immediately before the air-strikes, less than a week, five or six days before the air-strikes, and this was an indication that the bombing would start and we all expected that to happen. And there was an escalation definitely, although this fact was quite well-known, that we were to expect the angel of mercy quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the terrorist attacks did escalate in that period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please do not go to any length.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, on the 15th of March it had already been made clear by the NATO Alliance that we would be bombed, and the OSCE mission withdrew at that time. We knew what was going on and the terrorists attacked everything that belonged to the Serbian people and to the Serbian state with all they had, it was an all-out attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague Mr. Lukic asked you about the resubordination, and you described the situation, the events with Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Dikovic in your contacts and I want to know what you yourself did regarding the resubordination. Did you receive any orders from your superiors in the MUP regarding this issue?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me just tell you very briefly, this is what I pointed out to Lieutenant-Colonel Dikovic, that I as such and as a member of the police force in an ethnically pure area, that I would be happy for us to operate in this manner but that I had not received any orders to that effect and as a professional I had to comply with the orders and rules of my service, so it was immaterial. And I explained in the previous question that apart from the uniformed part of the police I also had the auxiliary services that served the needs of the local population, issuing ID cards, passports, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you did not receive any orders about the resubordination?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom we've seen a lot of documents from the Army of Yugoslavia about the humanitarian aid delivered to the population in the Glogovac area. Did you together with the army personnel take part in this and did you provide humanitarian assistance to civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we did, definitely. We had extraordinary cooperation in this regard, and this is something that I'm proud of to this day. Lieutenant-Colonel Dikovic organized everything on behalf of the army, gathering aid. I don't know in what way we did that, but he did gather the supplies and he delivered it to the people, to the people who had fled, the people that we and the army were trying to turn back to their homes and we did receive an instruction that was an obligation in effect from the Pristina SUP that we had to -- we had to provide any kind of assistance to the civilians, logistic support, food-supplies, accommodation, and that's what we did. And let me stress once again, our assets were limited. We didn't have enough food for ourselves and we made do in all kinds of ways. We wanted the Pristina SUP to get more food-supplies to us and we also used some local sources for food. And through some people that we trusted, we put in place this distribution system and the army did the same under the leadership of Lieutenant-Colonel Dikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 5 -- P1996 up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, to speed things up, you see here on the screen the minutes of the meeting held at the MUP staff in Pristina, the police -- senior officers in the police. And now I will go to the words of Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need page 9 in Serbian or in B/C/S and that would be page 11 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So regarding the clear-up operations, let's deal with that issue. Could you please look at paragraph 3: "Configuring the battle-field: Continue clearing up the terrain ..."

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can understand this as a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will ask you the question, if you allow me. You will agree with me that the clear-up operation of the terrain was in the jurisdiction not only of the local authorities but also of the police, but that you did not have sufficient resources to actually do it, you personally, as the chief of the Glogovac OUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may comment on this to say that this is the minutes of the 7th of May, and at that time I was not at the Glogovac OUP anymore and I think that any comments that I might make might be superfluous. On the other hand, as far as I know regarding the period while I was there at that post, the regulations in force stipulated that the officer in charge of the combat operation was the one who was also charged with doing the clear-up operation. So as far as I know, on the 7th of May, because I did go back to Glogovac from time to time to return some of the equipment. So I did have some knowledge, I learned at the Pristina SUP that my colleagues did go out into the field to do the clear-up operation. I don't know the details. I don't know how far they went, but I'm sure that they did comply with what is stated here in the minutes of the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, you will agree with me that the control of public law and order, safety of persons and property, control of the roads were among the key tasks of the MUP even during the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in peacetime and in wartime the police always takes care of that to save the life and limb of the people, the property. So these were the basic competences. This was what the police is for, but force majeure is force majeure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, you will agree that the territory of Glogovac, or rather, the control of the territory was carried out by two PJP detachments that were not under your jurisdiction, the 36th and the 86th Detachment of the PJ, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If I may elaborate were headquartered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If he wants more information, he'll ask for it. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we please see 5D -- 5D1417 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the title because we don't have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The disposition of the PJP in the territory" -- just a moment. The image is moving. "The disposition of the PJP in the area on the date of the 17th of April, 1999, and the secretariat in Pristina, and then it says 1st Company Banja Malisevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you just read out the companies?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fine, 1st Company Banja Malisevo, 2nd company Gornja and Donja Fustica; 3rd Company Kriva Reka, Nekovc -- could you please scroll down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, yeah, that's fine. 1st Company, Banja Malisevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 36th PJP Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 36th PJP Detachment. 1st Company Banja Malisevo, 2nd Company Gornja Fustica and Donja Fustica, 3rd Company Kriva Reka, Nekovc --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we're not going to go through a cut-price translation of documents in this way. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received the answer. I just wanted to get the confirmation for the axis where the forces of the 36th and the 86th Detachment were deployed, whether they were deployed in those axes in the municipality of Glogovac as read out by the witness right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has he given you that answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did say that they controlled them, but I can speed everything up with just one question and the witness can give us a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Damjanac, lest we should waste anymore time. The 36th and the 86th Detachment, all those axes that are listed here are in the Glogovac area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Damjanac, now regarding the check-points, you probably know that the Army of Yugoslavia provided direct security in the areas of deployment of its units in order to prevent any unauthorised personnel from entering those areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that at those joint check-points the military police personnel were in charge of checking military vehicles and military personnel, while the police was in charge of checking other persons and other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is according to the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Damjanac. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Damjanac, you'll now be cross-examined by Prosecutor, Mr. Oren. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: When you told us about your career in the beginning of your testimony yesterday, I don't think you told us which position you had in the OUP of Glogovac, but during your testimony I understand that you were the chief of the OUP in Glogovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I may have omitted that, but -- because I assumed that it was something that everybody knew in advance, so I didn't stress that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And you also told us that you worked in Glogovac until the 1st of May, 1999. Why did you resign as chief of OUP in Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the simple reason, as I indicated there, because of the physical and the mental burden of the previous leadership, a replacement had to be made and it is up to the superior officers to decide and to assess who might be appointed to that position in such a tricky situation, which is definitely not a laudable one. And I was familiar with the mentality of the people there and that's why they decided to appoint me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But my question was: Why did you resign at the 1st of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you're wrong as our brothers, Croats, would say. I did not resign. I was pulled out of Glogovac and that was the decision of my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So it was your superior's decision, it was not the result of a prior incident or anything in Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that we got the wrong interpretation twice, and that's why we're now having these problems because my colleague said why did he left this position and the interpretation was why he was appointed. And then the question was: Why did you resign? And the interpretation was: Why did you resign. So we get a wrong interpretation in Serbian, which is what we are listening to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know why you were removed from Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, were you promoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you demoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was quite acceptable in the Serbian armed forces at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you answer the question. Were you demoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you ask why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did not get a fair answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as they say in our parts, everybody gets -- everybody answers for their own honour. I don't know what the interpretation of this proverb is going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly not an answer to my question. Is that acceptable, that you get no answer when you ask for a reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not acceptable, but the then-chief did not deign to provide me with a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you not able to challenge that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I act as a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did say that you did not get a fair answer. What was the answer that you got?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the answer that I got was that allegedly I had not punished my "komandir," because according to what my chief said he had been getting drunk every day and that had resulted in some conflicts with the police officers. The only thing that I managed to say to this superior of mine is that this was not true because the "komandir" that he labelled as a drunk, he was actually -- he actually suffered from diabetes, a very serious case of diabetes, and he had never drank a drop of alcohol and that was the question and that was the answer and this was the end of the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you sent daily reports to your superiors in SUP Pristina, informing them of all important issues. Could you be more specific about name and rank of the person you reported to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was quite precise yesterday. According to the chain of command Bosko Petric as chief of the secretariat was above me; and his absence it was Bozidar Filic. So these were the only people that I reported to and nobody else. And the other sections were connected laterally with some other services in the secretariat of the interior in Pristina according to their areas of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And when you started at Glogovac, how did you know whom to report to? Were there written orders or instructions regarding who to report to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way that the service was set up to function indicated there existed the subordination. I report only to the officer who is my superior, and those who are under me report to me. So I submit reports to the leadership of the secretariat, and they provide information to me through the channels, appropriate channels, about the actions and so on depending on the actual situation. So I would provide proposals in some cases, but I could not decide. The chief of the secretariat was the one who decided, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren, can you find a suitable point to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Yeah, just one more question and I'll be there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And you also said that you informed your superiors about all important issues; and the nature of that information that you were to report, was that specified to you in any way, either written or orally?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was liberal in deciding what was important and what was not important for the secretariat, so if my cleaning lady doesn't come in today and the place is a mess I'm not going to report to the chief about that. But if there are any demonstrations, unrest, any murders, this is something that the secretariat would be informed about and we would seek feedback from them as to what to do in any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But my question, Mr. Damjanac, was whether they were specified to you in any way, were there like written orders, instructions, or similar?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, no -- well, the question is not really clear to me but I say no. I used my discretion to decide that because it was left up to the chief to decide, but I really didn't understand your question. You have to be more specific. Tell me about some problems and then I will tell you whether it was reported now that we're talking about this communication system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was whether there were any rules or guide-lines determining on what matters you had to report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to have our break at this stage, Mr. Damjanac. Could you leave the court with the usher, please, and we'll see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I please have P1991 in e-court, and if we could have page 4 of the English version and page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Damjanac, this is a record from the meeting of the ministry staff of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, that's what it says on the first page, and it's of 21st December 1998. On page 3 in the B/C/S version at the very top could you please read that paragraph to me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bosko Petric, Pristina SUP, briefly stated that the security situation -- briefly said that the security situation had worsened to a small extent especially in Glogovac and Podujevo municipalities, that they had drafted a plan to combat terrorism and that it was mostly being implemented."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And Bosko Petric, that was your superior, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about this plan he refers to, to combat terrorism, and that it was mostly being implemented. Do you have knowledge of such a plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the system, according to the obligations and the instructions that we have to comply with, we always do an annual plan depending on the crime growth trends in some areas. So there definitely was a plan to fight terrorism because we do annual plans to fight ordinary crime, fraud, economic crime. But there definitely was the plan to fight crime too because we're a serious service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And did you take part in the drafting or planning of such a plan that Mr. Petric refers to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to be so kind and to show me this plan, I could give you a definite answer, but otherwise I would have to speculate. I would like to see what the plan is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: If I could have P3116 up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And if I can have the assistance of the usher I can give you a hard copy of this. We don't have this in English translation, so I'm afraid you have to read out a bit from it. If you go to the first page, could you please read the first page to us.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The plan of the internal affair -- department of the interior in Glogovac to combat terrorism."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And if you go to the last page, and could you read from -- I guess there is a line where there is a date included. Could you read from there and the rest of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Glogovac, 11 number, there is no log number or protocol number, but at any rate the date is the 4th of December, 1998. "The plan was drafted by OUP chief Major Petar Damjanac, and the plan was approved by the secretariat chief, Colonel Bosko Petric."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And that's the same Bosko Petric as we have been talking about before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And when it says the 4th of December, 1998, and the previous document that you saw, minutes from the meeting of 21st December 1998, do you agree with me that most likely it's this plan that Bosko Petric talked about and stated that it was mostly being implemented?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I can only make claims from my area of jurisdiction. I assume that he presented this plan at the meeting where he was present. I was not present. And I am not familiar with the minutes and I am not familiar with the entire situation regarding the staff, so to be quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But after the 4th of December this was being implemented, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that's fine, but I don't know about the procedure from then on; but up to that time, everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But do you agree with me that when you look at those dates, 4th of December and 21st of December, 1998, could it be this plan he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably among other things. I say "among other things," he had to go to any meeting well-prepared, that's what we all did and that's what we all do, and he had to have this plan at hand in order to be able to present the whole situation in the Glogovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And you drafted this plan yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Were you alone or did somebody else work on this plan as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't type, I can't use the new technology, so I had to get a police officer to type it up and "komandir" Radovan Laskusic was with me as an experienced "komandir" with over 40 years of experience. So we drafted this whole plan, we made the draft, and then we submitted it to the secretariat chief in its final version for his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But concerning the content of the plan, was that only you or was it also your colleague that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that the OUP is a small work community and we in the leadership, we consult and we work together, all of us together; but I as the chief of the OUP, I decide. I drafted it, but I did that in consultation with my "komandir" because we had to plan the use of the uniformed police in the OUP and that is something that was closer to his purview because he was in command of the uniformed police in the OUP. I don't know if I'm being concise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, who ordered you to draft this plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders, "nalog," come from my superior, in this case it was Bosko Petric, the security assessment in the Glogovac municipality. That was the question that I received. Please provide a security assessment of the situation in the Glogovac municipality, and that was what I was required to do and all the other chiefs and all the other OUPs in the municipality, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were ordered to do this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably a few days before this, and it was probably conveyed over the special telephone line, dedicated telephone line. It must have been at least a week because that was the time that would be needed to put all this together to prepare everything because it requires a lot of work and effort and it was not an urgent matter. It would not be something that would have to be dealt with in one day or two. Maybe it was about a week before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Do you remember why you were ordered to do this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in accordance with the Rules of Service. Let me say once again, any problems that pertained to the work of the service had to be regulated in a plan, the so-called security assessment. Since the burning issue in Kosovo was terrorism, I was merely told to do the plan to suppress or combat terrorism, just as I had been told to do plans to combat drug addiction, car thefts, we had all kinds of actions. I don't have to enumerate all of them or to tell you what their names were. But other plans were made analogous to this plan and they were submitted for approval of the superiors, and in my case the superior was Bosko Petric.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 2, could you please read out the two first paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bearing in mind the current security situation in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, and in particular in the municipality of Glogovac, where in the town itself all the major facilities of the local administration are located as well as the premises of the OUP, the PTT -- the Serbian PTT buildings, the train station, the health care centre, and other facilities in this area, such as the DD Feronikel, the DD Jukodrenica," that would be limited company just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for the benefit of our clients, if we could have that particular part of the -- on the e-court, I'm sorry, because it is not what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where -- why is there no --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is page 2, first and the second paragraph but this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is there no English of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: I just came across it a couple of days ago and there were no time for an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you mean you just came across it a couple of days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wasn't aware of it until that when we assigned on this witness and that's all the information I have regarding that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've had it translated, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: I have had one from the people assisting me to go through it and what is said, but I have not like an English translation in paper of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we now have on the screen the part that's being read, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was there when I last checked. It's been moved again, so it has to be the second page of the document, first and the second paragraph. That is what my learned colleague was -- that's it. Thank you very much. I'm sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, could you continue reading that, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned those facilities such as the Feronikel joint-stock company, Jukodrenica joint-stock company, Kosmetrans transport company and the Grmija department store. Certain security measures are hereby proposed. And then should I continue, those measures are now listed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
