utterances.text: Yeah, could you read the second paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When all those facilities are being protected, it is necessary to organize the -- to organize coordinated action of our forces with the members of the state security sector and the Army of Yugoslavia personnel, lest they should be occupied by the so-called KLA which so far has strong strongholds in the entire territory of the OUP and in particular in several villages around Glogovac and the broader area. The OUP buildings are in the very centre of Glogovac and it is very difficult to organize the defence of those buildings because they can be accessed from all directions, and in particular from the privately owned homes, houses, that are located next to the very building and in the broader area."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Damjanac, are you on paragraph 3 now?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Only the second paragraph I told you to read, so thank you. Regarding the second paragraph, you are mentioning the VJ and the state security sector. Now, who were you in contact with within these units when you drafted this plan?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say once again, this is a plan that I personally drafted, I and my immediate circle of associates, "komandir" -- in fact, I and the "komandir" drafted this plan, and this plan, as any other plan, depending on the situation, the assessment, and so on, we propose something. Now, whether this would be accepted or not, this is outside of our jurisdiction. We don't make decisions. We only make proposals, the valid proposals, and the only valid proposals are the ones that we made because with 25 or 30 police officers we could not defend the Drenica region or the state of Serbia for that matter and to protect the integrity of the country, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So your answer is that you were not in contact with any members of the VJ or the state security sector; is that it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 4 of this document, and if you could please read out the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's where it says forces and equipment and materiel that are being proposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the conditions of a direct attack, we consider that it would be sufficient to engage the existing forces with all of their weapons with the use of light artillery weapons and armoured fighting vehicles with the full coordination with artillery units of the Army of Yugoslavia that are currently stationed in the broader region of the Krivovo village and Gornja Korotica village, and next to the quarry near the Vasiljevo village."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And the assessment of using light artillery, was that also your assessment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was all a matter of assessment, nothing outside of the assessment, and in fact the name of this plan is the assessment. Nothing can be done outside of the assessment, because the army was a respectable force and with their assistance we could save ourselves in case of an attack and we could save that part of the territory. That was the essence of our assessment, nothing outside of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And you -- or the plan is mentioning certain VJ units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying here that with the assistance of the Army of Yugoslavia, because as I said we were very small and we couldn't defend the police station and our lives in that area, and much less to protect all the facilities in that area and to defend the integrity of our country. So in case of an attack on the integrity of our state, then it was our or my assessment, if I may say so, it would be necessary to engage some of the units of the army deployed near the municipality of Glogovac or in the territory of the Glogovac OUP, and I mention here the sector of the Krivovo village where there are some army groups. That's all I say. The village of Krivovo, Gornja Korotica, and near the quarry by the village of Vasiljevo. So they were concentrated in a narrow area. Those were groups of troops that were located there. I don't know if I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: If we go to the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing I'm not clear about. You said that -- something about in the case of an attack on the integrity of our state it would be necessary to engage some of the units of the army. Now, that sounds rather different from an assessment of the security situation with a view to dealing or combatting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my interpretation. I consider that to be an attack on the state. That's my personal interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but your -- it says, according to the English translation: "In the case of an attack on the integrity of our state ..." and we commenced this section of the evidence by reference to the minutes of a meeting on the 21st of December, where your superior was reporting on this plan being implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Right at the beginning I said that I couldn't comment on the meeting of the staff that I didn't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just ignore the fact --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ignore the fact that you were not at the meeting. We want to know what you experienced, and the question is: Were you aware of this plan being successfully implemented in the month of December, the same month as it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This plan was probably used only by Chief Petric at that meeting for the purpose of that meeting. It was implemented to the extent possible, the capabilities of the OUP Glogovac and its cooperation with other state authorities. So it was implemented, but to what degree, that's now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's now what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know yourself from what we've said so far, that the terrorists at one period held 90 per cent of the territory in the municipality of Glogovac up until the 25th of July, when in the period from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is December, Mr. Damjanac. Please do not sidetrack the issues that we're dealing with at any given time in your evidence by referring to other events, which simply causes confusion in everyone's mind. Let's deal with December 1998. We've got -- you almost -- well, we've got an opportunity here to deal with a specific period of time. Now, in your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I simply went back in time of up until the time when the OSCE arrived. After the arrival of the OSCE, the terrorist forces went back to their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. No, no. I've asked you, as has Mr. Oren, a very specific question. Was the plan that you drafted being successfully implemented in the month of December?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This plan was being implemented, but this plan envisages that in case of an attack on the police station how to fight back, how to save all this. In case of a frontal attack, or rather, there was no frontal attack by the Siptar terrorists on the police station in this period of time, frontal attack from -- a full-on attack from the axis that was assessed as the major risk. So the army units were not engaged. This was just a hypothesis, a hypothetical plan if something happens what should be done. Some things did not happen, and then those measures were not implemented. I don't know if I'm clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the next page, that would be page 5. Could you please -- have you found it, Mr. Damjanac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Could you please read the first whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the event of major hostile actions directed at Glogovac, it is to be expected that the main action would come from the direction of Banjica village. In that case it would be necessary to engage the artillery unit or an artillery unit of the VJ which would from its current position open fierce fire targeting the positions and strongholds in that direction and more broadly in the area of Globare, Trstenik, and Poluze villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: When you said that it would be necessary to engage the artillery unit or an artillery unit of the VJ, were you capable of making such an assessment on when to use artillery?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is said very precisely here: "In the event of major enemy actions, hostile actions, in the -- targeting Glogovac," that is, when it becomes indispensable, it's the last resort when they are threatening to kill us, we cannot just go bare-chested against their machine-guns and the most sophisticated equipment that they had procured by that time from the NATO Alliance and others supplies, whereas our weaponry was reduced to 7.9-millimetre calibres. We can only go against birds with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is that you are capable of making such an assessment of when to use artillery; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to interpret your words. I'm saying again, only in the event of major enemy action targeting Glogovac, only in that case, in case there are major enemy actions we would request that an artillery unit of the Army of Yugoslavia be engaged because without that we would all be destroyed, we would just be killed off like sitting ducks. That is our request, it's more of a request than anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Okay. The last paragraph I want you to read out is the next one. Could you please read that one to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, now in this he's not merely suggesting that there will be need of the army artillery, he's also proposing what they would be doing. So how does he appropriate to himself a position like that, he said they'll be firing from this side and so on and so forth. I mean, that is something you wanted to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question to him was if he was capable of making such an assessment that this paragraph states, and -- because he said that he did not have communication with the VJ when he compiled or drafted this plan. So my question was merely on his competence on this specific topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What I was thinking was that he make -- could make a request because of the impending danger, but could he also suggest what they were supposed to do? I mean, that's what he's done. That's -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Well, I guess you heard what the -- what His Honour said, what the Judge said. Do you see this as a request or is it an assessment from your side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just an evaluation which is very customary in police work. I was not entitled to make requests, I was not entitled to issue orders. I had no influence over the personnel up the chain of command in the secretariat of the interior, and even less so on the Army of Yugoslavia which is independent, has its own place in the constitution, and has its own rules and coordination. I from my viewpoint have the right to propose what can be done to combat regular crime as well as terrorism in the area of Glogovac municipality. Whether anyone would acknowledge it or take it into account -- I mean, I could say anything. I could say that it's a good idea to film it all from a spaceship, make precise pictures, and then come up with our own plans --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would give them a good laugh but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. There's no need for frivolity in here. It's a serious business we're engaged in. Mr. Lukic, you have some comment to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because with this translation we have his answer that he could not make request and he could make the request. The reason why we have this confusion is the two Serbian terms were translated with "request." "Moliti" and "zahtevati." He was telling us that he could "moliti" kindly ask, I would rather translate it, he could not request. So the second time when he said "we couldn't request" is actually request. The first time it wasn't request, it was only to ask for something, if possible, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I think the sense of this is clear. Mr. Damjanac, the matter that's concerning the Bench is that you in your capacity as a senior police officer can actually write in a report how the VJ would be engaged, what they would actually do, without ever speaking to them, and that notion seems very strange to us. Would you like to comment further on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I'll try to make it clear once again. If it were a report, I couldn't say any such thing, but in a contingency plan where I can propose what we should do if they move forward to kill us all and endanger the territory of the state, it's just my proposal. I would not retreat from this then or now. It's just a plan, my initiative. It was not within my competency to make an application for or demand or decide. This is just a work product, a working material, background material forwarded to my superior that was used at a meeting of the staff. He just used passages from this to explain how serious the security situation was in the area of Glogovac and its environs, and I don't see in this plan that it was even approved, I don't even see my signature. Maybe it was just -- this is just a print-out from the computer. I'm not denying that I wrote this. I could sign it now, but it's just my personal view, my proposal. Whether anybody would acknowledge it or not is beyond me. There's no signature of Bosko Petric, so if you look at this from a legal standpoint, this is not a legally valid document. It was not even registered properly. Anybody can play with a computer and print out whatever they want, but my proposal was to act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you suggesting somebody's played with a computer and printed this out. Is that your serious suggestion here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't rule out that possibility. I'm saying this is a working draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this was not the final version; is that what you're saying? I mean, let's be clear about what exactly you are saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be a working version. What I'm saying is I don't see the final format of the text, I don't see the registry number, I don't see the signature. The way it looks now, it's not a document, I'm just commenting on this paper, on the wording, on the language, I am not commenting on the document. We are all lawyers here and we know what a document is as opposed to a text. It could be a love letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be my omission, Mr. Damjanac, but did you say that you were a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have you practiced as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in the police. I worked mainly to combat economic crimes, white-collar crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren, do you have any further part of this that you seek to have read?

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Only the next paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please do that and then I'll come back to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, could you please read out the next paragraph on page 5?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The weaponry and other combat assets currently at the disposal of the PJP which are at this moment located on the premises of joint-stock company Feronikel in Glogovac and the police station of the OUP are sufficient to defend the facilities where units are quartered and to inflict at the initial stage considerable losses on the terrorists in case they attack -- in case of attack on the terrorists."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In case of attack on the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So this rule says the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would -- I'm sorry. I think that the meaning of this is attack on the facilities of police, not on the terrorists, the last part of the para that was read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read the paragraph again, please, Mr. Damjanac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The weaponry and other combat assets currently at the disposal of the PJP which are at this moment located on the premises of joint-stock company Feronikel in Glogovac and the police station of the OUP are sufficient to defend," I repeat, "defend the facilities where units are quartered and to inflict in the initial stage large losses on the terrorists in case they are attacked," meaning the facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Mr. Lukic is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So this means that the PJP had weaponry and other combat assets in the Feronikel factory, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are policemen, not fishermen, of course they have the necessary light weapons to defend themselves and the facilities where the units are accommodated. The police station of Glogovac where we are and the other facility, that is a part of the Feronikel installation where the other policemen are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Do you know what weaponry and combat assets the PJP stored in the Feronikel factory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Feronikel factory there was the weaponry envisaged by the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, nothing more, that means light infantry weapons of the 7.9-millimetre calibre and certain, let me say conditionally speaking, combat armoured vehicles that would protect personnel as they tour the terrain or they use roads that are under siege, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And it was your assessment that this weaponry was sufficient to defend the facilities, as it's stated in this paragraph? You were not in contact with the PJP when you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, and to the first part of your question I would also like to answer. As you remember, we were attacked by 50 terrorists the previous day, the 11th November, and we managed to defend ourselves with our light weapons. You think they were a very brave, strong army? Even now we could defeat them with those weapons and drive them to Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you stated that from May 1998 when started to use this factory to accommodate some of the forces, you said. Now, was it these PJP units you referred to then?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From end May, yes, I mean precisely those units. They rotated every month, maybe two months, I'm not sure. At the beginning it was two months, later on they rotated every month.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: As you used the word "forces," were there also other units accommodated in this factory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "forces" I mean pejoratively and adequately. Forces are both police and army troops. That's what I meant by forces. I don't know what other terminology I could use. That's what I meant. I don't know if I was precise in using the word "forces," but that's what I meant, units of the police, units of the army, they are some kind of forces as long as they are uniformed and both of them are and they have weapons. Even the hunting associations are a force of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me rephrase my question then. As you said from May 1998 until the 1st of May, 1999, when you left Glogovac, were there other than the PJP units that used the Feronikel factory or was located there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, save for the personnel that was properly accommodated there, those units from the Kragujevac area, from the broader area of Sumadija region in Serbia. Nobody else had the ability or the right to use the premises of Feronikel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have more questions for this document. You said you had another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the very beginning of this document. Could you please, Mr. Damjanac, read the first paragraph that you see in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In view of the current security situation in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, and especially in the area of Glogovac municipality, where all the most important facilities of local self government are in the town itself as are the quarters of the OUP, the postal services of Serbia, the railway station, the health centre and other facilities in this area such as joint-stock company Feronikel, joint-stock company Jukodrenica, Kosmetrans business and the department store of Grmija, the certain security measures are hereby proposed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then could you go to -- in fact, just read the beginning of the next paragraph, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In protecting all the aforementioned facilities, it is necessary to organize coordinated action of our forces with the members of the state security sector centre and the Army of Yugoslavia so that these would not be occupied by the so-called KLA" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You read that before. Now, could we go to the very end of the document, please. Not that page, the very end of the document. Can you read the last paragraph, that's the one before the space for the date, the one above that, it's three lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "This plan is subject to change and amendment depending on the security situation on the ground. Any amendment hereto requires approval from the staff of the secretariat in Pristina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that in July 1998 it was launched an anti-terrorist action, a joint action by the army and the police and that for the first time between mid-July and September, as you said, all the roads were now cleared and all the strongholds of the Siptar terrorists were crushed throughout the Drenica territory and the area was finally liberated. Now, I guess that during these actions a number of detainees were brought into Glogovac OUP for interrogation, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Were there any investigations or cases in Glogovac against members of the MUP regarding mistreatment of persons taken into custody in this relation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We need to all understand one thing. It was a time when the state of war had not been proclaimed yet. We acted exclusively under the law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of a single case of mistreatment, if that's what you mean, that would require investigative action, although we are not the ones who would take such action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was that the situation for the whole of 1998 and up until the 1st of May, 1999, when you left Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And you never received reports, information, or even heard rumours that such things had happened?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. There was not a single report in any form of that kind, either written or oral, and unless I am informed of something I cannot know it, unless it's reported, at least if not to me, to the service where I'm working.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Yeah, because as a chief of the OUP you will of course receive information if such incidents had happened, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If that was registered in the log-book, I would know unless it would be a sabotage by my own policemen. There's order and discipline. If there was an incident that was registered, we should have acted upon it. I should have been notified to see what the issue at hand is and if there is a crime of lesser importance, so to say, it will be forwarded to the inspectors to follow it up. As the chief, I couldn't have controlled each such case involving certain elements of a crime; I had administrative tasks to attend to for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Are you aware that members of the security service sent information to the VJ security administration stating that unidentified members of MUP units carrying out combat operations in Gornje Obrinje in September 1998 executed persons taken into custody? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never notified of that case. I wasn't informed. Some Finnish pathologists and the Pristina SUP told us that some people should go to Gornje Obrinje, including an investigative judge. What was mentioned that a family had been killed, that was the first time I got by some general information; otherwise, I wasn't specifically privy to any such case. I only remember that initiative taken by the Finnish pathologists, and again that was under the purview of the Pristina SUP and not for Glogovac to do anything about it. They were supposed to be taken up to the location, and we were not notified of any further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But I guess you were aware of the operations going on in Gornje Obrinje in late September 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: It is a large municipality and we had no physical contact with the area of Gornje Obrinje. It includes Gornje and Donje Obrinje, Likovac, and so on and so forth and it was a KLA stronghold. The actions undertaken by the PJP and the military, well only they knew about it and they wouldn't let the local regional police stations know about what their intentions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did Gornje Obrinje not fall within your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Gornje. It is a border area. Administratively speaking, Gornje Obrinje was in Glogovac municipality and Donje Obrinje was a part of the municipality of Srbica and then we have Likovac nearby, but it was a single area for the KLA. It was their stronghold and many of our forces didn't even dream about entering that area until it finally took place in what was it? July or August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm only trying to be clear about this. If Gornje Obrinje falls within your area, why was this not a matter that fell within your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For security reasons. We could not get to the inner part of Glogovac. That is the essence. The centre of the KLA zone for the area of Demonica [phoen] was precisely in Likovci and Obrinje. With 25 to 30 policemen we couldn't against thousands of them, we couldn't go there. Even before you reach that, there must have been at least 20 check-points, trenches, communicating trenches, and so on and so forth. As the head of some 25 or 30 men, my primary concern was to take care of their lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When do you say that you first learned of this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Finnish pathologists - I'm talking now without consulting any documents, I can't tell you exactly when it was, I do believe you have that in the documents, at least the Prosecution does - it was when the Finnish pathologists tried to reach Gornje Obrinje together with an investigative judge and the police. I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That helps. You told us yesterday, I just can't find the note at the moment, though, about another event in Gornje Obrinje. Do you remember the other incident you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean murders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. And I will repeat, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could, please, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in January 1998, Mustafa Kurtaj who was a PTT employee of their office in Glogovac was shot, he was killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a forest worker, forestry worker, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, he worked for the postal office, he was a postman. Sejdi Musa was the forest worker, but that took place afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that also Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sejdi Musa was killed in Gradica. In Gornje Obrinje a father and son were killed. Nobody talked about the father since the case wasn't reported, but I do know that Rexhep Kurtaj who was the father of the late Mustafa Kurtaj was killed a week later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it does appear that on the 26th of September a number of people were killed in Gornje Obrinje. You say that at that time you knew absolutely nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have the document to see who the persons killed were. Ten years later my memory's failing. There were 32 policemen killed in the area of Glogovac. The number of those that were injured or the combo was twice as much and I won't even go into any other figures. Some were kidnapped too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Members of the Delijaj family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was interpreted to me was Delijaj. That last name doesn't exist I think either among the Serbs or Albanians. It is probably an interpretation error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the name we have. D-e-l-i-j-a-j.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a different matter, Your Honour, it has to do with the Finnish pathologists, that particular case, that's it, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. My question to you is: Had you heard absolutely nothing at all about that prior to being told by the Finnish pathologists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never, none of us at the Glogovac OUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, in connection with these operations in Gornje Obrinje were there people brought into Glogovac police station for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the police station of Glogovac, or rather, people were taken in from the area of combat. They would be brought in in trucks and they wouldn't tell us exactly who hailed from what village. They would simply deliver them, literally speaking, and then we would register those people. And it would be at that point that we would learn who came from what area. That included all sorts of locations, not only around Glogovac, but from, for example, the municipalities of Klina and Srbica as well as Lipljan. As to what they were all doing in that area, I won't go into commenting that. However, the fact is that they were found in the area. Maybe they were shepherds and he may have been Klina and was found in Glogovac. They were all found there. I don't know to what extent you're familiar with it, but these were all able-bodied men. They were not taken in in uniform, that's true, but usually under the uniform they would wear sweat-suits and immediately when in danger they would discard their weapons, their uniforms, and would turn civilian, and then it would be up to us, the policemen, to try and establish whether they were members of the KLA or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And these persons that were brought there, they were detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't accept the term "prisoner" or -- we never declared war on anyone. If there is no war, there is no prisoner --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second. I think that my learned friend used the correct term in English, but translation was incorrect. I think that it should be corrected "pritvorenici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's ask the question again, please, Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: These persons that were brought in, they were detainees, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that some of the detainees were beaten during interrogation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Wasn't the engine of an armoured personnel carrier turned on in order to drown out the screaming?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are stories. It is absurd for me to even consider those, whose screams, what screams, chicken, what? Let's see who it was, let's see a document, who said what. Whose screams and what sort of a vehicle it was that was revving outside. Our police station is a pre-fab building, 10 by 5 metres inside. Please, you're confusing the people and I have problems with my blood pressure. You want me to die here today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, Mr. Damjanac, offhand, but in the indictment in this case there are many people listed who lost their lives in Kosovo, there are hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Kosovo. I'm only talking about my area, of Glogovac. As for the rest of Kosovo, I cannot provide any explanation. I told you beforehand that I had 32 policemen were killed, twice as many seriously wounded. I won't even go into the numbers of casualties among civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, your flippancy here is not appreciated. Please bear that in mind. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Perhaps a question to lower your blood pressure. Yesterday you told us that all questioning were done at the police station in Glogovac, and then you were asked --

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And then you were asked whether your OUP questioned someone in the Feronikel factory and then you answered the following: "The people in that factory on the premises of that factory had their own supervisory bodies and we had different jobs. We were in charge of regular police work and their job was to provide security for certain installations, buildings, and roads, so we did not coordinate mutually and we did not use the premises of Feronikel for any official procedures." Now, first, when you used that phrase did you have any unofficial procedures in the Feronikel factory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is imprecise, unclear. What do you mean unofficial? Throughout my work in Glogovac, during that period I only went to the Feronikel factory twice because of certain incidents which had taken place, and once I was there because the electricity had been cut off. There were no formal or informal meetings with them. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: The question was simply when you use the term "official procedures" if that was your intention, in relation to that you had unofficial procedures in the Feronikel factory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No unofficial procedures in our contacts with the Feronikel factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Do you know if other units than OUP Glogovac interrogated or detained persons in the Feronikel factory?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know - and I'm convinced I know enough - no one was using the Feronikel facility for any interrogation of any parties or to detain them or anything in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You referred yesterday, as Mr. Oren has pointed out to you, to people who were providing security at Feronikel. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SJP [as interpreted], as I said yesterday, and I repeat it today, they came from central Serbia, they came there to assist, they came with their own leadership and were responsible and answerable to them. Of course should they require and need help, it would be normal that we would provide that and the other way around if we were attacked. There is a distance of 1 kilometre between the Feronikel factory and the police station in Glogovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me again who they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People who came from Serbia proper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the name you gave; the initials I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the PJP, Posebne Jedinice Policije, to provide security of facilities and they were the so-called B version, they were not there to combat terrorists but to provide security to facilities, to man check-points, to secure roads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- state buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were asked when you were head of the Glogovac OUP if there were any mass departures of civilians from the area of your municipality and you stated that there was no such thing and people didn't even think about it. Now, today we have heard about some people leaving, I think that's what you meant. So my question is: When you stated that no civilians left your municipality at all, is that really what you mean or is that as you interpret the term no mass departure of civilians took place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you what, exceptions do not make a rule. I said what I knew. I said that on my approval or my order or on the basis of principles I used for the work of the OUP in the area, there was no need or reason for the population to leave. Quite the contrary, they should have stayed and shared our fate. I said that yesterday and I'm saying it today. Of course there were individual cases. If I lived there, I would have escaped with my family as well, but those were exceptions. I tried to explain that yesterday. Members of the KLA who were members of their families and immediate circle around their leaders, of course they wanted to stay in the Drenica area. But I don't know of anyone going to Albania or Macedonia while I was there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, I've cut off your microphone. You're not answering the question anymore. Please listen to the questions and answer them. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question then. Say in March/April 1999, were there civilians leaving Glogovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat, perhaps individually, not collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: And those who did leave, how did they leave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you an example, by your leave. Fadil Dervishi, conditionally put, he was a loyal citizen of Glogovac municipality. He had a bar in the centre of Glogovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've cut off your microphone again. The question is: How did they leave? Could you answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking now about the individual cases, but nothing collective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there no general way in which people left? Did they walk? Did they go by vehicle? Where did they go? That's what we're interested in. Now, there must be some -- is there a general pattern or is there not a general pattern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat it yet again, and I would kindly ask the interpreters to interpret word for word. During the time that I headed the OUP in Glogovac, there were no group departures of Siptars --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, your answer was translated perfectly well, that people left individually but not collectively. Couldn't be -- it's a nice simple answer, one of the few simple answers you've given us. Now, the next question that follows from that is: How did they leave? How, h-o-w in English, how did they leave? Could you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would go to Pristina in their private vehicles. People -- there were no buses there, no trains, no city transport, nothing was working, only private vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's easy if you just listen to the question. Concentrate your mind and answer the question you're asked. We'll now break for lunch. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll resume again at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Oren, please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Just before the break you told us that while you were in Glogovac you didn't know anybody going to Albania or Macedonia and you also said that there were no buses in Glogovac. Are you aware that there are reports claiming that residents in the centre of Glogovac was informed on 24 April 1999 that buses would be arriving to take them to Macedonia if they wished to go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from the beginning, and I have to repeat again, there was no collective moving out from Glogovac municipality for as long as I was the chief there. Whether a letter like that exists, a report, I don't know, I had nothing to do with it and I don't know anything about it, but there was no collective moving out because I was very much opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about buses leaving Glogovac around the time of 24 April 1999 heading for the Macedonian border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Did you ever advise people to leave Glogovac in this period of time, around 24, 25, and 26 of April?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to explain that by that time I had already started to hand over my duties, and it never occurred to me, never crossed my mind, to advise anybody to leave Glogovac. So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Are you aware that there are reports claiming that the police on the 26th of April went door to door in Glogovac, telling residents that there were two buses going to Macedonia and that they were free to stay or go? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Are you of the opinion that the police in Glogovac could guarantee the safety of the Kosovo Albanian population in this time-period?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I could guarantee my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: So your 25 to 30 policemen in uniform was sufficient for this purpose, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again from the standpoint of security of the citizens we persuaded to stay, we guaranteed that we would defend them till the last drop of blood and they could come to harm only over our dead bodies. But ultimately, whether we would succeed in protecting ourselves and them, only God could tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: But you were of the opinion that you and your 25 to 30 uniformed policemen could guarantee the safety of the Kosovo Albanians, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are talking already about April, the time of air-strikes, the situation when there were no longer any terrorists. With the terrorists out of the picture, we could guarantee their regular security, just as we did before the conflict, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Was there any question of the military to take over the area of Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: You never told people that, that the army could take over the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that nor did anyone say that to me. I'm hearing this for the first time from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At what date, Mr. Damjanac, had the terrorist threat been removed from Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, practically, save for constant air-strikes, they had already pulled out to other areas close to the borders and Glogovac was not troubled by terrorism too much for those two months during the bombing. There was much less aggression from terrorists than before the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Oren.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Are you aware that there are reports claiming that approximately 200 residents were told that their safety could not be guaranteed if they remained and that they were given 15 minutes to decide whether they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OREN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a number of questions for you, Mr. Damjanac. You said that once the OSCE arrived your police could only move in 100 metres diameter. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may sound strange, but it's true. Apart from the road from Pristina and from the intersection at Komorane to the police station in Glogovac, we could not move any further for the simple reason, as you could see from the document shown some time ago, that Sami Lushtaku prohibited us from using the road, which means that we couldn't do our job properly, we couldn't send our patrols anywhere near. And I will take the liberty to tell you, and it's up to you to judge. After this representative of the OSCE, this German man aged around 55, insisted -- I told you his name yesterday but I've already forgotten I'm afraid, it was a bit provocative I think but he invited me to tour their premises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point is it was not an official restriction, it was a practical restriction; that's really what I wanted to be clear about.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, that was the problem, because they came to me every day and warned me against going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Kosovo was there any system for recording the ownership of houses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because quite frankly, the area of Drenica is more than 97 per cent populated by Albanians. There was a very small number of Serbs. We knew exactly which flats they occupied and the workers' hutment next to the police station, the OUP. The only thing they didn't wear was the yellow David star on the sleeve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you misunderstand my question. I'm anxious to know whether when a person owned property, but in particular a house, in Kosovo there was a register in which he was recorded as the owner of the property.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cadastre service exists, now that I understood your meaning, it exists like in every other country in the world, it holds records of titles to property everywhere, that's true, and this cadastre service is attached to the municipality if I got your meaning correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when houses were burned, why were you unable to identify the owners?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my time in the area where I was, I don't know which burned houses -- I don't know whether any houses were burned during my tenure in the area where I and my policemen were able to move. On the other hand, we have to bear in mind another fact. It is true that the cadastre holds records of titles to property, but 90 per cent of housing is built illegally without proper permissions, and that's true unfortunately not only in the Drenica area. It's the state of affairs throughout Kosovo and Metohija to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave us evidence of groups of civilians being escorted back to their homes. Is that something on which you submitted reports to the chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an obligation that required no particular procedure. It didn't have to be reported specially. I remember escorting around a hundred people in Karkas when the army brought them. It was found that they were all ordinary citizens and they were all released --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you just answer my question. Did you report to the chief of the SUP or not when you were aware of your policemen escorting large groups of civilians back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, he was informed of everything. The chief of SUP was informed of everything. I don't know whether all the documentation from that time was preserved, but the courier took written reports every day at 4.30 from Glogovac to Pristina and he carried documentation both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be I've misunderstood what you were saying a moment ago, but in the case of the hundred people in Kark as, was that reported to the chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim with any certainty, but I think he was, he was informed, and the unit that was there could confirm probably. I cannot say with any certainty, it was too long ago. But I think everybody knows, the citizens remember this, and I think I filed the report as well but I can't know for sure. There were thousands and thousands of reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In light of what you said a moment ago about the drop in terrorist activity when the bombing began, why were the army in your area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely to protect people, to protect buildings, roads, and everything. They split into groups and they acted like guerilla warriors in the hit-and-run fashion. They could hide easily after every attack in the hills, in the woods. They had moved away from the urban area of Glogovac, and that's why we were more at peace for a while. But they remained there in mountainous positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't want to oversimplify the evidence in the case, but the sort of activity you've just described is not activity we have heard of the army handling in this case. My question is: Why were the army in the area in the period after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I tried to explain, first they were there to finally free all the roads, to break all the terrorist strongholds, to control the broader area from and prevent incursions and attacks by terrorists from all sides. Without their help, we would have been unable to do anything. And there's one other thing, we were facing the NATO aggression at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm trying to avoid -- clear up any misunderstanding from your answers, and one of the things you said to Mr. Cepic was that when the OSCE pulled out, which is more or less coincidental with the start of the war, the terrorist attacks escalated. And a moment ago you told me that the terrorist activity decreased substantially when the bombing started. I'm trying to understand these two statements, if you can help me, because they don't seem to fit with each other.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the urban part of Glogovac, that is the point. Because of police and army presence, they withdrew into hilly areas where they have natural camouflage and hiding places. They were no longer in the urban area of Glogovac and we could breathe a little. Until that time we were unable to step out of our police station more than 50 metres. We couldn't effectively cover our territory. We didn't know within a circle of 100 metres whether there were any terrorists out there advancing on the OUP. With the arrival of the army, we could breathe a little. The army had work to do. They had to fight, they had exchanges of fire, skirmishes, but we could relax a little, we could go to work in peace, go back home without being attacked. We could do our regular work with citizens and the citizens were also able to breathe a sigh of relief at that time. But in the mountains meanwhile fierce fighting went on with terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, two questions arise from yours and I hope you will allow me to put them to the witness. One of them has to do with the reason why the army came to his area, and the second one relates to the units mentioned in the document shown by the Prosecutor, that plan from December 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Damjanac, it's me again. Could you tell me, at the beginning of the war was there a threat of a ground invasion by NATO into Kosovo from Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common knowledge that a ground invasion was possible. Unfortunately, you didn't ask me this before, I would have liked to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, in that document that was shown to you earlier called the plan, the units of the Army of Yugoslavia were mentioned, Krivovo village, or rather, the quarry near Vasiljevo village. My question is: Is this close to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as the quarry in Vasiljevo is concerned, that was a stronghold of the KLA in Vasiljevo and then the army freed us of it and secured the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Another question, Mr. Damjanac: Do you know if a VJ unit was there in that area to protect the road coming from Pristina under the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Damjanac, the end is now very near. My colleague Mr. Aleksic showed you the document 6D579 regarding those ribbons, and I would like another document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the name of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give the number again, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's 6D1473. And we'll need point 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see this on the screen, para 6?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want it in Serbian because I'm not an Englishman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have it in your binder, maybe it's easier to look it up there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6D1473. Could you please read para 6.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ensure adequate marking of the member of the -- of the members of the brigade by red ribbons that will be requested and supplied in sufficient numbers by the assistant commander for logistics of the brigade. The ribbons shall be tied and worn according to an explanation to be provided in due course."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us the date.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the signature is what?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Ljubisa Dikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The one you told us about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see those ribbons in the field?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 3 -- we don't need this document anymore, you can close the binder, on page 32, line 3, my learned friend Mr. Cepic asked you who was responsible for enforcing the law and maintaining order. You answered the police, and I would like to ask you if there were any areas on the territory of your OUP that were not under the control of your police. You said territories held by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to say that the entire evidence I have given so far indicates that we controlled effectively a very small part of the territory of Glogovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any areas in your -- in the coverage of your OUP that were controlled by the army?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the areas where they had their quarters, where we didn't go, the army held that and of course they controlled that area, such as Domenik. We didn't need to pass by that way, that's where the army was stationed, it was one of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we will need 5D1417.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have that document, so you will see it on the screen. We never really established who wrote this document, but here in the handwriting it reads: Questions 4: The detachment commander, members of the staff, chief of the SUP. Then 1: Deployment of MUP units: When they arrived there, staying until when, on which locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, these notes in the top right corner in handwriting, that's something that we wrote, our Defence team wrote while preparing it. Unfortunately, this copy was entered into evidence like this, although I have asked my assistant to provide another clean copy. This is something that we used in our preparations and it just went in by mistake like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that clarify it for you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'm even more confused now, and I would ask at this moment that use of this document is not allowed until it's corrected and all questions posed based on this document would be withdrawn from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document is confusing completely. I think that we -- at some point was even this handwritten part discussed and it's misleading, and if provided by the Defence of General Lazarevic, we would kindly ask the source who compiled the document. We don't know yet what this document is at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only matter raised was whether it showed the presence of PJP detachments in the Glogovac area, which the witness had already confirmed before the document was put before him. I don't think anything else was asked, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure now whether he -- at least we would like to know the source of the document, who compiled it, when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your comments will be noted and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we accept that it ought to be replaced, but it's not possible to ignore what has been said in relation to it unless you can show that that would give rise to some risk of injustice. And while that could arise in other circumstances that hopefully will now be avoided, it's not immediately clear that any injustice is likely from the use that was actually made of the document. But you can return to it if you wish once you've had a chance to think about it when you have a chance to review the transcript. You can let us know if there's any other action you would like to take. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, we found this document in the electronic disclosure suite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's as simple as that, though, Mr. Cepic. If you then decide to found on it, you're the man that has to establish its authenticity. Since I've never been in the electronic disclosure suite, I don't know if it also includes other items which are there to ensure there's no accusation of withholding material, but in relation to which there may be dubiety about the authenticity. So the onus is on you now that you've decided to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is already the second witness who confirms the relevance of the information given in the documents. Before him I asked Colonel Mijatovic, and he gave the same answers regarding relevance. And I would like to get your permission to replace in the electronic -- in the e-court this document with a clean copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, once you have one you can -- I think you should make a written filing in this instance, and that would give Mr. Lukic an opportunity to respond to it before we decide what to do. But for the moment we're stuck with this one until there is a clear issue for us to resolve. Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we now call up in e-court P3116.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have seen this plan of the department of internal affairs in Glogovac to combat terrorism and you were asked whether it was in fact implemented on the ground in whole or in part. How much territory at that time in December 1998 was held by the KLA in Glogovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to go back to the beginning, it was practically in control of let's say 90 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in which part of the territory -- you said the plan was implemented. In which part of the territory were you able to implement this plan in December 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to make this point again. This plan was made towards the end of the year. We only applied it from Komorane until Glogovac and Globare, and we controlled an area of a couple of villages. That's what we could do. Stankovci; Komorane; Donje, Gornje Zabelj; Poklek; Novi and Stari Strbulovo; Glogovac town; and Novo Cikotovo and Staro Cikotovo, that's what we were able to do with the resources we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was terrorism envisaged as a crime by the penal code?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as one of the gravest crimes. A case file was made for each incident, forwarded to the public prosecutor's office, and prosecutions went on until the last day when all the case files were turned over to UNMIK, whose duty it was according to the agreement to continue working on all the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it part of your regular police work to detect all sorts of crime, including terrorism?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding this plan, do you know whether your chief, Petric, actually did something about this plan. Did he do something about coordinating with the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, he did not inform me about that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the PJP unit quartered in the Feronikel factory was engaged to hold observation points along roads according to the agreement with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DAMJANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Damjanac. Thank you for coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: If we look at page 9, line 1 to 20, you talk about people, detainees as you call them, who came to this police station where they were screened, whether -- to check whether they were amongst those who had targeted the police and you administered the paraffin tests. Now, I was trying to inquire that did you -- was there anybody supervising this activity or it was totally at the discretion of yourself or anybody else you may have picked out for this purpose to declare that, yes, this man is the one who should be sent to the security forces for further action and for trials or -- and these are the people who should be let off. Now, what was the -- what was the method of verification, so that was a little anxiety I had in my mind. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Your Honour. Just one note, this document was not shown to me at all and I'm talking off the top of my head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: It's not a document. Please open up page 9 of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Okay. Forget that, it's just a general question then. I mean, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as a general question I will answer it. I think I already did, but let me repeat. The OUP in Glogovac did not have this special service, the crime technician service that would be finding physical evidence of crimes including the gun-shot residue tests, which is known widely as the paraffin test. The expert team was called from the Pristina SUP. This is not something that I wanted or that I ordered. So from the service of the interior, a special team specially trained, qualified team is engaged and on the basis of the physical evidence they were able to ascertain that those people had handled fire-arms, used fire-arms. And that made us process these people further. They were taken to Pristina, and then somebody, the competent service either from the state security or from the public security sector, processed these people further, tried to establish facts, find evidence to the effect that they were really members of the KLA, and then if it were to be ascertained that they had committed any crimes, then they were prosecuted. I don't know that, what happened to them. I know that about 2.000 people were amnestied by our prime minister, including the Mazreku brothers, and some people who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm now aware of what you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Damjanac, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence called Miomir Bogosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sit down, please. You'll now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bogosavljevic. First of all, for purposes --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, for purposes of the record I would like you to give us a brief introduction and overview of your essential biographical details.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miomir Bogosavljevic, I was born on the 18th of July, 1952, in Donje Petric, Klina municipality in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm married, father of three, and I have three grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And at the beginning of my questioning I should also caution you that there will be times when there will be a pause, that's not because I don't understand your answer; it's just that we have to wait for the transcript and the translation to catch up with us. Now, could you very briefly give us an overview of your schooling and educational background.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in my place of birth and secondary school of internal affairs in Sremska Kamenica. I graduated in 1971, and then I completed school in 1986 -- actually, in 1971 I was enrolled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've already mentioned the school of internal affairs. Could you please briefly provide us with the details of your work history within the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: After completing the secondary school of internal affairs, which was in 1971, I started work as a traffic policeman in the traffic police office of the provincial secretariat of the interior in Pristina. After completing the college in 1986, I was appointed to the post of inspector, carrying out the on-site investigations of traffic accidents. In 1992 I was appointed the commander of the police station for railway security at Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you still work within the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. After the police withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija in 1999, I transferred to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade. And then in 2005 I retired. It was a regular retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, just to be clear you did mention when you became the commander of the police station for railway security at Kosovo Polje. I'd like to ask you specifically about the years 1998 and 1999. What specific position did you hold within the Serbian MUP at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I was the commander of the station, commander of the police station, for railway security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And within the line of work of the police station for the security of the railway station at Kosovo Polje, to whom within the MUP did you report; that is to say what structure within the Ministry of the Interior was your superior to whom you were responsible?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was responsible to the chief of the police department at the Pristina SUP and his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us during the relevant time-periods of 1998 and 1999 who were these specific individuals from the SUP Pristina who were your superiors?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time the chief of the police department was Zarko Brakovic and his deputy was Vesko Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as the work of your police station for security at the railway station in Kosovo Polje, did any entity called the MUP staff or staff of the Ministry of Interior in Pristina have any effect or role in your work at the Kosovo Polje police station for security?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, except for the police department in the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So am I to understand your answer that the police department of the Pristina SUP was your -- was the only entity that had any effect on your daily work, is that -- am I reading what's reflected in the transcript correctly, is that what your answer was?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reported exclusively to them. I was responsible for my work and work of my station, exclusively to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to reports later on.
