First of all I want to ask you, since you mentioned that you were appointed as commander of this station in 1992, did you notice any change in the work of the station or of the organs in the SUP that you had dealings with at any time after the establishment in June of 1998 of a MUP staff that was headed or managed by Sreten Lukic as the "rukovodilac" which again means head or manager, that changed the work of your station or the SUP at all?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated when you were appointed to the position of station commander at the police station for security in Kosovo Polje -- in the railway station in Kosovo Polje. Who within the Ministry of Interior had the authority to appoint you to that position and how did this occur?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed the commander of the police station for railway security at Kosovo Polje at the recommendation of the Pristina SUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say upon recommendation of the Pristina SUP chief. Who in fact was empowered to make the actual appointment based upon this recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the public security sector of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the other employees of the police security station for the railway station in Kosovo Polje, would the procedure be the same for them as it was for you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. For the deputy commander and the assistant commander, their appointments were handled by the Pristina SUP chief, he appointed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And are we to understand then that the Pristina SUP chief could do that on his own without any higher authority within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He could not do that for my appointment, but as far as the appointments of my deputy and assistants are concerned, he could do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could just take a few moments to talk about discharges -- potential discharges of duty. What would -- who could discharge you as the commander of the police station for public security at the railway station in Kosovo Polje? And while you're answering that question if you could also tell us what -- whether -- whether the same would be in effect for other employees of that station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My discharge is done on the basis of the proposal of the Pristina SUP chief, and it is done by the chief of the public security department of the Serbian MUP. As far as my deputy and the assistants are concerned, this could be done by the Pristina SUP chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could focus just on disciplinary matters for -- potential disciplinary -- potential disciplinary matters for any employees of that police station for security at the Kosovo Polje railway station. Who had authority for discipline?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were minor and serious infractions of work duty. For minor infractions, any sanctions were handled by the Pristina SUP chief; and for those major ones, it was done by the disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now could you tell us a little bit about the structure of your police station for security at the Kosovo Polje railway station, and including in your answer the manpower that was available for you to use at that stage in conducting your duties.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the systemization, the station was supposed to have 66 police officers including the commander; but the staffing level was only up to 50 or so per cent. We had 37 police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say you had 37 police officers. Did these police officers work all at once or did they work according to shifts?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, they worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the number of police employed at this station change at all during the course of the NATO attacks and the war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could focus on these 37 police personnel. I say "personnel" because I'm not sure that they are all men. Do you recall if within the ranks of this -- your police personnel, the security station of the Kosovo Polje railway station, if there were any members of non-Serb ethnicity employed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were people of other ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, without yet telling us the exact names, did these same persons stay on employed at the police station even during the time of the NATO war?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the war they were still there, but they left later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, at this time to ask one question -- ask one or two questions which have specific names of these individuals, I would ask that we go into -- is private session the least restrictive of the sessions? The reason being is these individuals are of non-Serb ethnicity that worked for the police, if they are in Kosovo could be subject to reprisals. We've heard evidence from other witnesses in these proceedings of the measures that were taken against personnel of non-Serb ethnicity that continued to work in the police and other non-governmental organs. So for the potential safety of these third parties, I would ask that we go into the lesser restrictive -- I believe private is the lesser-restrictive session just for two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, is there any problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to ask you: Were there any members of the RDB within the police security station at the Kosovo Polje railway station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the work and duty or authority and jurisdiction of your station, could you please explain what that was during the relevant time-period so that we can understand the type of work that you did.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The police station for railway security had its tasks - now I'm talking only about trains - to ensure the safety and security of passengers, to prevent any breaches of law and order, to prevent the commission of any crimes, thefts, illicit trade, forcible stopping of trains, and it was there to provide assistance to the railway personnel on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are we to understand from your answer then that police officers would ride on the trains; and if so, approximately on average how many of the 37 police officers you earlier stated you had in your station would be on a given train at a given time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: On every train that would be one patrol consisting of two police officers in the course of a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, what about the actual train station itself, under whose jurisdiction and authority was the security of the train station itself?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: All railway stations in the territory where the railway line passed are in the jurisdiction of the appropriate, relevant police stations and secretariats according to the territorial principle. So I only had to secure the trains. The security on the train was within my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You earlier mentioned reporting. Could you explain for us what types of reporting existed that your station had a duty and obligation to undertake and to whom that reporting was sent?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were urgent, daily, and periodic reports. I only reported to the police department in the Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just briefly jump ahead in time to 1999 and specifically the period of the NATO air war, how was the reporting affected, how was it able to be undertaken at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Urgent reports were sent by phone or by radio communications up until the time when the air-strikes began -- or, in fact, up until the time when the Pristina SUP building in Pristina was hit when the radio relay station there was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How was your reporting with the police department in the SUP Pristina undertaken at that point in time when all those other forms of communication were curtailed by the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: After the building was hit, couriers were used to carry reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, specifically focusing on the work of your station, would you receive plans for that work, how frequently, and from what entity or source would you receive plans for the work of your station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the work-plans for my station, those were drafted solely by myself based on the general guide-lines received from the chief of the police department of the SUP in Pristina. That would be received towards the end of the year in order to plan for the next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the physical location of your station, prior to -- could you please tell us, prior to the NATO bombings where it was located and then whether that position remained the same during the course of the NATO air war or if you were relocated somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The railway security police station was in Kosovo Polje itself, in one of the buildings belonging to the railway company. At the beginning of the NATO aggression we were relocated to a private home in Kosovo Polje where we remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was your family with you during the NATO bombings or were they elsewhere and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, 1999, my family went to Serbia because of the fear of the NATO aggression once the KVM had left Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll talk about some other persons who left a little bit later. I'd like to focus now, according to the regular practice and procedures relative to your police station, from whom would you be able to receive orders?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Orders? Why? What orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the work of the station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think I've already replied to that. It came solely from the chief of the police department at the SUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to attend any meetings at the police department in SUP Pristina during the period 1998 through 1999, especially dealing with these orders or plans of work as being the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I frequently attended meetings at the police department of Pristina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during these meetings were the persons there exclusively from the SUP Pristina or did you have occasion to ever witness anyone from the MUP staff in Pristina participating in any way in such meetings regarding the functioning of your station and the SUP Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the meetings at the police department that I attended, the persons there were all commanders of other police stations. We would meet with the chief of the police department, his deputy, and several other officers working at the police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please tell us which railway transport routes and lines were covered by the policemen and women of your police security station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The routes we covered were as follows: Kosovo Polje-Kraljevo; Kosovo Polje-Pec; Kosovo Polje-Prizren; Kosovo Polje-Djeneral Jankovic; and Kosovo Polje-Kursumlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you able to actually follow all trains on all these aforesaid lines in all directions during the time-period 1998/1999; and if not for any of them, why?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In most cases we covered all trains. It seldom happened that there was a train without police escort, since on occasion we were short of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the course of undertaking their duties, if a police officer discovered that criminal act had been committed either by eye-witnessing the same or receiving a report from someone of the same, what was the normal and regular procedure followed by your police station in reacting to such events?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If there was a crime committed on board the train and if someone would report that to the policeman there, he would note that down, he would record it officially and would also try to do something in order to detect the perpetrator of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as commander of this station, do you recall receiving any large -- any large number of complaints about mass theft from the civilians that were boarding trains there in 1999 during the course of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. During 1999 I can state that not a single crime was reported to me or any of my policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did -- did you or anyone else at your police station have any role or effect on either increases or decreases in the number of passenger cars or wagons attached to the trains that passed through Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. An increase in the number of cars or the number of special trains falls within the purview of the railway administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And a related question based upon your many years of service, generally speaking, if there was ever to be an irregular or not-previously-scheduled train, how would you be advised of the same and would you have any role -- would you have any authority to make such a decision?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Concerning the arrivals of special or not previously scheduled trains to Kosovo Polje, that's something I have never been advised of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I forget if we asked you to briefly describe the uniforms and weapons that the police -- that the police had when conducting their duties and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I just -- before you go on to, that's a completely different subject, ask two questions. Is Kosovo Polje effectively the main station for Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pristina has its own train station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is the station -- or in 1999 was the station in Pristina more important than the station in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not. Kosovo Polje is a hub.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And from Kosovo Polje were there no trains which crossed the border into Macedonia regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the routes you gave us did not include any route that went beyond the boundary of Kosovo itself I think -- no, no, there were some but none went beyond the boundary of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Djeneral Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that line goes to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But did the trains regularly run from Kosovo Polje to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did until the beginning of the NATO aggression. My policemen and women only went as far as the train station in Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I forget if we had asked earlier, if you could please -- actually, let me just see whether -- yeah. If you could describe for us the uniforms and weapons that your police had or were given for purposes of conducting their work, and if there were any reasons for the same.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Until May 1998 they wore only blue uniforms and side-arms. As of May when Albanian terrorists began being active in the vicinity of the railway going to Pec, the policemen began wearing blue camouflage uniforms and long-barrelled guns on all routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there instances of threats or interruption of service of the trains by the KLA during -- at that period or any period thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the route between Kosovo Polje and Pec on several occasions they entered the train and mistreated the passengers. As of May the train moved without police escort. I believe it was in May when a policeman was kidnapped from the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. You previously mentioned radio communications and the lack of effect during the NATO bombings. The hand-held radio stations that you did have, what was that equipment's range as used by your policemen?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The radio devices used by my policemen had a very short range. Probably because of the amount of metal on the train, radio communication could only work close to SUP centres when a train would pass by and the range would only be that of a couple of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you notice following the KVM withdrawal, which occurred approximately the 20th of March, 1999, but before the NATO bombings when it was already I think known in the media that the bombings would occur, did you notice a change in the passenger traffic at the Kosovo Polje train station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Once the verification mission left there was an increase in the number of passengers in the direction of Macedonia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you or the policemen working under you have occasion to have any contact with some of the civilian travellers who were leaving at this time and did you have occasion to talk with them explicitly about the reasons for their departure and travel? And for purposes of this if you could give us as much specifics as possible.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My policemen did have contact with the passengers and I had contact with the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us about your personal contacts and the specifics of that contact, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Should I mention the names of the people I spoke to or only the details of the conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought this person was no longer in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, for the safety of a third party since this is one individual -- one individual and multiple other individuals, I would have one question in private session. I apologise, I would have done it earlier if I'd realized that there was the possibility that some of these individuals might be back in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall go privately -- briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. Could you describe for us some of the targets and the intensity of bombing by NATO aircraft in the Kosovo Polje region?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo Polje, in addition to the freight railway station, another building was hit with a projectile but it wasn't damaged seriously and the lines remained intact. There's an airstrip in Slatina which is 5 or 6 kilometres away from Kosovo Polje and it was targeted daily as well as the barracks in the outskirts of Pristina in the direction of Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as someone who lived in Kosovo Polje at the time, could these explosions at the Slatina airport that occurred every day, could they be heard and witnessed from Kosovo Polje itself?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, the distance between Kosovo Polje and the Slatina airport is about 2.000 metres. One could see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, returning to your station, did your station ever receive any type of order from your superiors in the police to participate in any type of forced boarding of Albanian civilians onto trains for purposes of deportation from the region?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. My personnel was exclusively in charge of the train in movement. As I said a moment ago, the authority of the policemen working on railway security does not lie with the facility itself, the train station, but rather with trains in movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if in fact -- strike that. If -- did you receive any orders from superiors within the police to undertake theft or mistreatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How would such behaviour on the part of policemen have been reprimanded or reacted to by yourself as the commander of the police station -- the police security station?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If someone reported such an act, that policeman would be arrested and a criminal report submitted against him. He would also be suspended from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you during the time-period of 1999 during the NATO war have any reports of any multi-ethnic conflicts between the civilians of various ethnicities on the trains; and if so, what would have been your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR BOGOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were no inter-ethnic conflicts during that period. Had there been any, I would have undertaken appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the 3.30 point. I have about 10 to 15 more questions and will be brief in direct tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can interrupt at this point then. Mr. Bogosavljevic, we have to bring our proceedings for the day to an end at this time, which means you'll have to come back tomorrow to complete your evidence and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom. Overnight, between now and then, it is a strict rule that you have no communication with anybody at all about any aspect of evidence in this case. You must confine your discussions with people to subjects other than the evidence in this case. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 7th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
